title: Can you look like Kratos from God of War in real life? (RAGNAROK WORKOUT)
summary: NH lays out three free programs in sequence for building a Kratos-like physique dominated by the upper back, traps and shoulders. First comes the novice 3-day 'Atreus' PPL with burnout sets, then a 4-day 'Bridge' that adds volume, then an advanced 'Kratos' upper/lower x2 plus arms day using nucleus overload. He closes with FAQs on rotations, supersets, failure, diet and how long to stay on each program.
claims: Kratos's look is replicable in a smaller version because it is upper body and especially upper back dominant; expect 10-15 years
He avoids video games himself because of past addiction issues but follows the lore
A three-day push/pull/legs-arms program is enough for a novice to progress
An 'or' in his programs means pick one exercise or rotate both across weeks (week A / week B), never both in the same workout
Burnout protocol: pick a weight you can do for 20 reps max, set to failure, rest 2 min, set to failure, rest 1 min, set to failure, rest 30 s, one last set
Burnout sets are junk volume placed at the end of a session to condition the traps and rear delts for the higher workload of the advanced program
Never do burnout sets with something like an 8-rep max; the 20-rep weight keeps injury risk low
Neck work never hurts and any man looks better with a thicker neck
Superset means doing two exercises back to back without rest, then resting 2-4 minutes before repeating
The push-up/ab burnout uses five sets to failure with 3, 2, 1 min and 30 s rests, since chest and ab volume is otherwise low
Many lifters get 'intermediate syndrome' by jumping from a minimal-volume novice program to a high-volume intermediate one; a bridge program is needed to acclimate
The Bridge adds a fourth day (Saturday arms) and makes Friday a pure leg day, increasing volume while staying below the advanced program
Stay on each program as long as you keep progressing, possibly more than a year on the novice plan; the bridge will usually be shorter, maybe 3-6 months
The Kratos program is upper/lower twice a week plus an arms day, training the upper back every day except arms day
Muscle priorities for Kratos: traps, shoulders, upper back, long head of triceps, lats, biceps, abs, forearms; chest modest; legs minimal
Horizontal pressing (bench, dips) causes most lifters' shoulder pain, while vertical pressing tends to be easy on and even restorative for the shoulder
Nucleus overload is easy, sub-failure work with a light weight on an already-trained muscle; it is not a burnout set and supplements rather than replaces hard work
Pyramid of priority: the first lines of each day (heavy compounds) give the most results; skip the last line's sets if short on time
An evolving rep range like 10-15 helps you hit failure and progress over time
For weighted chin-ups use few sets (3x6-8) with maximal intensity and a narrow rep window to prioritize adding weight
A proper arm day is a sneaky recovery day: minimal compounds, mostly isolation, low nervous system fatigue
With high frequency end each day with about 20% in the tank, and an arm day with about 40% left
You may swap exercises if the replacement trains the same muscles the same way (e.g. Z press or Arnold press for dumbbell press)
If supersets aren't doable for beginners, do one set, rest one minute, do the next, then rest 2-3 minutes; but don't drop supersets entirely or the Kratos program becomes three times as long
Train isolation to failure on every set; compounds to failure if safe, otherwise 1-2 RIR
The number one beginner mistake is training too easy
A skinny novice must gain weight slowly, eating slightly more to gain a little each week, transforming within 2-3 years; if fat, eat at maintenance or cut very slowly
Stop chasing novelty; the best bodies were built through consistency and you should stay on a program while it works
Stop asking how long it will take; skinny men who keep checking the clock are not committed
